5: However, you wouldn't know this from past reporting. In 2021, many major media outlets picked up an article by Alex de Vries called "Bitcoin's growing e-waste problem". De Vries was a Central Bank employee and PhD student at the time. The study, along with much of de Vries' work, has since been [[6|debunked]]. However, the damage was done, and many still believe that Bitcoin poses a serious e-waste issue.
7: There's a much bigger omission, which I only found by accident when I was interviewing a senior member of an e-waste recycling company.
11: ERS already has contracts with 5 of the top 11 Bitcoin mining companies in the world. It reports that most of the big players are "receptive to having a sustainable strategy in place to handle mining rigs that have been deemed obsolete."
24: In 2021, [[13|Nic Carter confirmed]] that as mining companies bought the then-new S19s to mine "around the clock", they often moved old S9 rigs to sites powered by intermittent energy sources such as solar and wind.
29: A 500kW load bank will set you back [[15|$28,490]] and exists only to turn surplus electricity into heat. An obsolete Bitcoin mining rig can do the same job. It puts retired hardware back to work instead of into the waste stream, and earns Bitcoin while it does. When renewable operators use obsolete Bitcoin mining rigs as a load bank instead, it's cheaper for them and better for the environment. And they can earn Bitcoin.
